Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The government is warning that taking the psoriasis drug Raptiva could result in serious brain infection and even death. Raptiva may cause a serious brain infection called progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases, and a possible fourth, of people diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva. "Three of those patients have died," the FDA said in a public health advisory. "All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years." None was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system. Raptiva's product labeling was revised in October to highlight a boxed warning about the risks of life-threatening infections, including PML. "At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug's risks," the FDA's advisory says. In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA highlighted the confirmed cases and promised to "take appropriate steps" to ensure that Raptiva's risks do not outweigh its benefits. The FDA also said it will ensure that patients "are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML" and that health care professionals "carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML." Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has gone further, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients taking the drug talk to their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday it asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding. The group's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined "that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine." It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be "closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection." "Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment," the agency said. Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells -- cells that help fight infection -- in the immune system. Those cells cause the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva "decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient's susceptibility to infections," the FDA said. The National Institutes of Health says the prognosis for PML "remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities." Around 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, which is incurable, the NIH says.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The government is warning that use of the psoriasis drug Raptiva could lead to a serious brain infection and even death.

Raptiva may cause a severe brain infection known as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The Food and Drug Administration cited three confirmed cases—and a possible fourth—of patients diagnosed with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) after being treated with Raptiva.

“Three of those patients have died,” the FDA said in a public health advisory. “All four patients were treated with the drug for more than three years.” None of the patients was receiving other treatments that suppress the immune system.

Raptiva’s product labeling was revised in October to include a boxed warning highlighting the risk of life-threatening infections, including PML. “At that time, the FDA directed Genentech, the manufacturer, to develop a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) to include a medication guide to educate patients about the drug’s risks,” the FDA advisory said.

In the advisory, issued Thursday, the FDA emphasized the confirmed cases and said it would “take appropriate steps” to ensure that Raptiva’s risks do not outweigh its benefits. The agency also said it would ensure that patients “are clearly informed of the signs and symptoms of PML” and that health care professionals “carefully monitor patients for the possible development of PML.”

Overseas, the European Medicines Agency has taken stronger action, recommending that no new prescriptions for Raptiva be issued and that patients currently taking the drug consult their doctors about an alternative. On Thursday, the agency asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally binding.

The agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use determined “that the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks, because of safety concerns, including the occurrence of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in patients taking the medicine.” It said patients who have been treated with the drug should be “closely monitored for neurological symptoms and symptoms of infection.”

“Patients who are currently taking Raptiva should not stop treatment abruptly, but should make an appointment with their doctor to discuss the most appropriate replacement treatment,” the agency said.

Raptiva, a once-weekly injection for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, works by suppressing T-cells—immune-system cells that help fight infection. Those cells are responsible for the skin inflammation associated with psoriasis. By suppressing T-cells, Raptiva “decreases the function of the immune system, which increases a patient’s susceptibility to infections,” the FDA said.

According to the National Institutes of Health, the prognosis for PML “remains grim; the disease usually lasts for months and 80 percent die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been reported. Those who survive PML can be left with severe neurological disabilities.”

Approximately 6 million to 7 million Americans have psoriasis, an incurable condition, the NIH says.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Federal officials are cautioning that use of the psoriasis medication Raptiva may lead to a dangerous brain infection and, in some cases, death.

The drug has been linked to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, a severe brain infection. The Food and Drug Administration said there have been three confirmed cases, along with a possible fourth case, of PML in patients who had received Raptiva.

“Three of those patients have died,” the FDA stated in a public health advisory. The agency also noted that all four individuals had been on the medication for longer than three years. None of the patients was taking any other therapies that weaken the immune system.

In October, the prescribing information for Raptiva was changed to include a prominent boxed warning about the possibility of life-threatening infections, including PML. According to the FDA advisory, the agency at that time instructed Genentech, the company that makes Raptiva, to create a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy, known as REMS, including a medication guide designed to inform patients about the drug’s dangers.

In the advisory released Thursday, the FDA drew attention to the confirmed PML cases and said it would “take appropriate steps” to make sure the risks associated with Raptiva do not exceed its benefits. The agency also said it would work to ensure that patients are plainly told about the signs and symptoms of PML and that medical professionals closely watch patients for any possible emergence of the disease.

Regulators in Europe have taken stronger action. The European Medicines Agency has advised that doctors stop writing new prescriptions for Raptiva and that people already using the drug consult their physicians about switching to another treatment. On Thursday, the agency asked the European Commission to make that recommendation legally enforceable.

The agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use concluded that, because of safety issues — including cases of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy among people taking the drug — Raptiva’s benefits no longer outweigh its risks. The committee said patients previously treated with Raptiva should be watched closely for neurological problems and signs of infection.

The European agency also warned that patients currently using Raptiva should not suddenly discontinue it. Instead, they should schedule a visit with their doctor to talk about the best alternative therapy.

Raptiva is an injection given once a week to adults who have moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. It acts by suppressing T-cells, immune-system cells that help the body combat infections. These cells also contribute to the skin inflammation seen in psoriasis.

By reducing T-cell activity, Raptiva lowers immune-system function and thereby makes patients more vulnerable to infections, the FDA said.

According to the National Institutes of Health, the outlook for patients with PML “remains grim.” The illness generally continues for months, and 80 percent of those affected die within the first six months, although spontaneous improvement has been documented. Survivors may be left with serious neurological impairments.

The NIH says psoriasis affects approximately 6 million to 7 million people in the United States and has no cure.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration warned that the psoriasis drug Raptiva may increase the risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, a rare but serious brain infection that can lead to severe disability or death. The warning followed the agency’s review of confirmed cases of PML in patients who had been treated with Raptiva, a medication used for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis.

PML is caused by activation of the JC virus, a common virus that usually remains inactive in healthy people but can cause life-threatening disease in individuals whose immune systems are weakened or altered. Because Raptiva affects immune system activity, regulators became concerned that long-term treatment could leave some patients vulnerable to this infection.

According to the FDA, three of the four reported patients who developed PML had been taking Raptiva for more than three years. Those three patients died. The seriousness of these cases prompted the agency to require additional safety measures intended to reduce the risk to patients and improve early detection of possible neurological problems.

The FDA’s actions included stronger warnings in the drug’s prescribing information, additional guidance for patients, and increased monitoring requirements. Patients receiving Raptiva were to be informed about the signs and symptoms of PML, which can include changes in vision, weakness, difficulty speaking, loss of coordination, confusion, or changes in personality. Health care providers were advised to monitor patients carefully and to discontinue the drug if PML was suspected.

The safety concerns also led to action outside the United States. European regulators recommended that doctors stop prescribing Raptiva to new patients, citing concerns that the risks of the drug could outweigh its benefits. They also advised physicians to review the treatment of patients already using the medication and consider safer alternatives where appropriate.

Raptiva had been used to help control chronic plaque psoriasis, an immune-mediated skin disease that can cause red, scaly, and painful patches on the skin. While the drug offered benefits for some patients, the reported cases of fatal PML raised significant concerns about its long-term safety, particularly because psoriasis is not usually a life-threatening condition.

Regulators emphasized that patients should not stop treatment on their own without consulting their health care provider, but they urged both doctors and patients to weigh the potential benefits of Raptiva against the risk of rare but severe complications. The FDA’s warning and the European recommendations reflected a broader effort to ensure that patients using immune-modifying drugs are fully informed of possible risks and are monitored closely during treatment.

**FDA warns psoriasis drug Raptiva linked to rare brain infection, deaths**

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is warning that the psoriasis drug Raptiva may increase the risk of a rare and often fatal brain infection, after reports of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, including deaths among patients who used the medicine.

Raptiva, known generically as efalizumab, is an injectable biologic drug approved to treat adults with moderate to severe chronic plaque psoriasis. The FDA said cases of PML have been reported in patients taking the drug, prompting stronger safety concerns and additional warnings for patients and doctors.

PML is a serious infection of the brain caused by the JC virus, a common virus that usually remains harmless in healthy people. In people with weakened or altered immune systems, however, the virus can reactivate and attack the protective covering of nerve cells in the brain. The disease can lead to severe disability or death.

Symptoms may include progressive weakness, vision problems, difficulty speaking, confusion, loss of coordination and changes in personality or mental function. The FDA has urged patients taking Raptiva to contact their health care provider immediately if they develop neurological symptoms.

The warning comes as European regulators have moved to restrict the drug’s use. The European Medicines Agency recommended suspending the marketing authorization for Raptiva, saying the benefits of the drug no longer outweighed its risks because of safety concerns, including PML.

Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune-related skin disease that causes the rapid buildup of skin cells, producing red, scaly, often itchy and painful patches. Plaque psoriasis, the most common form, can be mild, moderate or severe and may significantly affect quality of life. Treatments range from topical creams and light therapy to systemic immune-suppressing drugs and biologic medications.

Raptiva works by suppressing parts of the immune system involved in the inflammatory process that drives psoriasis. But that immune-suppressing effect may also make it harder for the body to control infections such as JC virus, increasing the risk of PML.

Health officials said patients should not stop treatment without first speaking to their doctor, but doctors should carefully weigh the risks and benefits of continued therapy and monitor patients for signs of infection or neurological decline.

The FDA said it is continuing to evaluate safety data and work with the manufacturer and international regulators. Patients and health care professionals were encouraged to report adverse events through the FDA’s MedWatch safety reporting system.

counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON —** Federal health officials are warning doctors and patients about serious, potentially fatal risks associated with **Genentech’s psoriasis drug Raptiva**, after regulators linked the medicine to cases of a rare brain infection and other dangerous immune-system complications.

The advisory from the **U.S. Food and Drug Administration** centers on reports of **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy**, or **PML**, a usually fatal or severely disabling viral infection of the brain. Raptiva, known generically as **efalizumab**, is an injectable biologic drug approved for adults with **moderate to severe chronic plaque psoriasis** who are candidates for systemic therapy or phototherapy.

## FDA findings: PML cases tied to long-term Raptiva use

The FDA said it had received reports of **PML in patients taking Raptiva**, including fatal cases. The agency’s review found that the affected patients had generally been receiving the drug for an extended period, raising concerns about the risks of long-term immune suppression.

PML is caused by reactivation of the **JC virus**, a common virus that usually remains harmless in healthy people but can cause devastating disease when the immune system is weakened. Because Raptiva works by suppressing parts of the immune response involved in psoriasis, regulators said patients may be more vulnerable to severe infections.

Symptoms of PML can be subtle at first but may worsen quickly. The FDA advised patients and clinicians to watch for:

- New or worsening weakness on one side of the body  
- Vision changes  
- Difficulty speaking or walking  
- Confusion or changes in thinking  
- Loss of coordination or balance  
- Personality or behavioral changes  

The agency said patients should seek medical attention immediately if such symptoms develop. Physicians were advised to discontinue Raptiva and evaluate patients promptly if PML is suspected.

## Broader patient risks: serious infections and immune complications

Beyond PML, the FDA highlighted broader risks associated with Raptiva’s effects on the immune system. The agency said the drug’s labeling reflects the possibility of **serious infections**, some of which may be life-threatening.

Reported or potential risks include:

- PML and other opportunistic infections  
- Bacterial sepsis  
- Viral meningitis  
- Invasive fungal infections  
- Worsening or new neurologic symptoms  
- Blood abnormalities, including low platelet counts  
- Severe psoriasis worsening after stopping the drug in some patients  

Because Raptiva alters immune surveillance, the FDA said patients taking it should be monitored carefully for signs of infection and neurologic disease. The agency also emphasized that patients should not stop therapy abruptly without speaking to their physician, because discontinuation can sometimes lead to a rebound flare of psoriasis.

## REMS labeling and risk communication

The FDA said Raptiva’s prescribing information includes strengthened safety warnings, including a **boxed warning** about the risk of serious infections, including PML. The agency also required risk-management measures under a **Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy**, or **REMS**, intended to ensure that prescribers and patients receive clear information about the drug’s dangers.

The REMS-related labeling and communications were designed to:

- Alert physicians to the risk of PML and other serious infections  
- Provide patients with a **Medication Guide** explaining warning signs  
- Encourage prompt reporting and evaluation of neurologic symptoms  
- Reinforce that Raptiva should be used only in appropriate patients  
- Support careful benefit-risk assessment, especially for long-term treatment  

Regulators said clinicians should discuss the drug’s risks with patients before and during treatment, particularly because PML may be difficult to diagnose early and has no reliably effective treatment.

## European Medicines Agency recommends suspension

The FDA advisory came as European regulators also moved against the drug. The **European Medicines Agency** recommended that Raptiva’s marketing authorization be **suspended** in the European Union, concluding that the medicine’s benefits no longer outweighed its risks.

The EMA cited the PML cases as a central concern, along with the availability of alternative treatments for psoriasis. European regulators said patients using Raptiva should consult their doctors about switching to other therapies and should be monitored for neurologic symptoms after stopping the medicine.

## Genentech and next steps

Genentech, a member of the Roche group, has said it is working with regulators and health professionals to communicate the updated safety information. The company has urged patients not to discontinue Raptiva without medical guidance and to contact their physicians if they experience new neurologic or infectious symptoms.

For patients, the FDA’s message is clear: anyone taking Raptiva should be aware of the symptoms of PML and other serious infections, report changes immediately, and review treatment options with a dermatologist or other prescribing physician. For clinicians, the advisory underscores the need to weigh Raptiva’s benefits in controlling severe psoriasis against rare but potentially catastrophic immune-related risks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**Regulators question Raptiva’s benefit-risk balance after PML cases**

*By [Reporter Name]*  
*[Dateline]*

U.S. and European drug regulators are warning that the risks of the psoriasis drug Raptiva may outweigh its benefits after several patients taking the medicine developed progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, or PML, a rare but often fatal brain infection.

Raptiva, known generically as efalizumab, is an immune-suppressing injectable treatment used for adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. Regulators say the same immune effects that can help control psoriasis may also leave some patients vulnerable to serious infections, including PML.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said in a public health advisory that it had received reports of “three confirmed and one possible case” of PML in patients using Raptiva. The agency described PML as “a rare, serious, progressive neurologic disease” that affects the central nervous system and “usually leads to death or severe disability.”

The cases have raised particular concern because PML has no proven cure and because the affected patients had received Raptiva for extended periods. Regulators said the emergence of the condition changes the calculation for a drug used to treat a chronic, non-life-threatening skin disease.

In Europe, the European Medicines Agency said its Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use had reviewed the safety data and concluded that “the benefits of Raptiva no longer outweigh its risks.” The agency recommended suspension of the drug’s marketing authorization and advised physicians not to start new patients on the medicine.

The EMA said doctors “should not issue any new prescriptions for Raptiva” and should review the treatment of patients already receiving it. Patients were urged not to stop therapy without medical advice because of the risk that psoriasis symptoms could worsen or rebound after discontinuation.

The FDA similarly urged clinicians to reassess patients taking Raptiva and to watch for neurological symptoms that could suggest PML. Such symptoms may include weakness, vision changes, problems with speech or coordination, confusion, or personality changes.

Regulators’ concern centers on whether Raptiva’s benefit — improvement in psoriasis symptoms — justifies exposure to a potentially devastating infection. While severe psoriasis can be painful, disfiguring and psychologically burdensome, PML is frequently fatal and survivors may have lasting neurological damage.

Raptiva’s safety had been under scrutiny before the PML reports. The FDA previously required a boxed warning about life-threatening infections, including PML, and other serious immune-mediated complications.

The new warnings add to pressure on the drug’s manufacturer and prescribers to move patients to alternative psoriasis treatments. Regulators said patients currently using Raptiva should contact their physicians promptly to discuss other options and should seek immediate medical attention if they develop neurological symptoms.

**Raptiva Safety Concerns Intensify After Confirmed Cases of Rare Brain Infection**

*By Staff Writer*

Health regulators have raised serious safety concerns about **Raptiva**, a once-weekly injectable drug used to treat adults with **moderate to severe plaque psoriasis**, after confirming cases of **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy**, or **PML**, a rare but often fatal brain infection.

Raptiva, known generically as **efalizumab**, was prescribed for patients whose psoriasis was severe enough to require systemic therapy or phototherapy. The drug works by suppressing parts of the immune system involved in psoriasis inflammation. But that same immune suppression has been linked to an increased risk of serious infections, including PML.

Regulators confirmed **multiple cases of PML in patients taking Raptiva**, including cases in people who had received the drug for extended periods. Some of the confirmed cases were fatal. PML is caused by reactivation of the **JC virus**, which is common in the general population but usually remains harmless unless the immune system is weakened.

The confirmed PML cases prompted warnings that the risks of Raptiva may outweigh its benefits, especially because psoriasis, while chronic and potentially disabling, is not typically life-threatening. Raptiva was eventually removed from the market in the United States and other regions after regulators and the manufacturer concluded that the danger of PML could not be adequately managed.

Medical experts said the cases were particularly concerning because **there is no reliable screening test to predict who will develop PML** and no proven cure once the disease occurs. PML attacks the brain’s white matter and can progress rapidly, causing severe disability or death.

Patients who have used Raptiva were advised to contact their health care provider, especially if they developed any new neurological symptoms. Warning signs include:

- New or worsening weakness on one side of the body  
- Vision changes  
- Loss of coordination or balance  
- Difficulty speaking  
- Confusion, memory problems or personality changes  
- Seizures or other unexplained neurological problems  

Health officials emphasized that patients should **not stop or change treatment without medical guidance**, because abrupt discontinuation could lead to worsening psoriasis or other complications. Instead, patients were urged to speak with their dermatologist about safer alternative treatments and appropriate monitoring.

Doctors were advised to stop prescribing Raptiva to new patients, reassess those already receiving it and transition patients to other therapies where appropriate. Clinicians were also told to remain alert for PML symptoms during treatment and after discontinuation, since immune-related complications may emerge even after the drug is stopped.

Raptiva’s safety concerns added to broader scrutiny of immune-suppressing biologic drugs used for psoriasis and other inflammatory diseases. While many biologic therapies remain important treatment options, regulators said the Raptiva experience underscored the need for careful risk assessment, patient counseling and prompt evaluation of any neurological symptoms.

For patients previously treated with Raptiva, the central guidance remains clear: **seek medical attention immediately for any new neurological symptoms and consult a physician about ongoing psoriasis management and alternative therapies.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**CNN Health — Public Health Advisory**

**Long-term Raptiva use linked to immune suppression and rare fatal brain infection risk**

Health officials are warning patients and doctors about serious safety concerns tied to long-term use of **Raptiva**, a prescription medication once used to treat moderate to severe plaque psoriasis.

The concern centers on the drug’s effect on the immune system. Raptiva, known generically as **efalizumab**, works by suppressing certain immune responses that contribute to psoriasis. But that same immune suppression can leave some patients vulnerable to severe infections — including a rare but often fatal brain infection called **progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy**, or **PML**.

PML is caused by the **JC virus**, a common virus that usually remains inactive in healthy people. In individuals with weakened immune systems, however, the virus can reactivate and attack the brain’s white matter. Symptoms may include worsening weakness, vision problems, confusion, difficulty speaking, loss of coordination, or personality changes. The condition can progress rapidly and may lead to severe disability or death.

Public health authorities say the risk appears to be associated particularly with **long-term use** of immune-suppressing medications such as Raptiva. Patients who have used Raptiva for extended periods are being urged to contact their healthcare providers immediately if they experience any new neurological symptoms.

Doctors are also being advised to carefully review the treatment history of any patient who has taken Raptiva and to monitor for signs of serious infection or neurological decline.

Raptiva was previously approved for psoriasis, but safety concerns — including reports of PML — led to major regulatory action and its removal from the U.S. market. Patients should **not stop or change any medication without medical guidance**, but anyone with a history of Raptiva use and concerning symptoms should seek urgent medical attention.

Health experts emphasize that while PML is rare, it is extremely serious.

**Warning signs to watch for include:**

- Sudden or worsening weakness on one side of the body  
- Trouble walking or loss of coordination  
- Vision changes  
- Confusion or memory problems  
- Difficulty speaking  
- Seizures or unusual neurological symptoms  

Patients with questions about past or current psoriasis treatments should speak with a dermatologist or primary care physician to review safer treatment options and any needed follow-up.
